passages.t: Call to God: healing for a broken city
passages.happening:
While Jeremiah is still confined in the courtyard of the guard, the word of the LORD comes a second time (verse 1). ‘Call to Me, and I will answer and show you great and unsearchable things you do not know’ (verse 3).

The houses of the city and the king's palaces are being torn down to defend against the siege ramps and the sword (verse 4). The Chaldeans will fill them with the dead (verse 5). ‘Nevertheless, I will bring to it health and healing, and I will heal its people’ (verse 6) and show them abundant peace and truth. God will bring back Judah and Israel and rebuild them (verse 7). ‘And I will cleanse them from all the iniquity they have committed against Me, and will forgive all their sins of rebellion against Me’ (verse 8). The city will bring God joy and praise before all the nations (verse 9).

In this place they call a wasteland, there will be heard again the sounds of joy and gladness, the voices of bride and bridegroom, and the voices of people bringing thank offerings to the LORD's house and singing that the LORD is good and his loving devotion endures forever (verses 10 and 11). Shepherds will again rest their flocks in every town of Judah, and count their sheep as they pass under their hands (verses 12 and 13).
passages.hearers:
The setting is the siege of 588 to 586 BC. Verse 4 describes a real defense: houses near the walls, royal buildings among them, were torn down so their stones could strengthen the fortifications against the enemy's earthen ramps. The city was tearing itself down to survive.

Into that, God promises healing. The sounds that Jeremiah had said would fall silent, the bride and bridegroom of 7:34 and 16:9, will be heard again.

The song of the thank offerings, give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, is the refrain of the temple psalms. It would be sung again in a rebuilt house. Ezra records that it was sung when the foundation of the second temple was laid.

Shepherds counting sheep as they pass under the hand was the evening count at the fold. Ordinary life will come back.
passages.later: The returned exiles sang this very song when the temple's foundation was laid (Ezra 3:11). It is the refrain of the psalms: ‘Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good. His loving devotion endures forever’ (Psalm 136:1).
passages.asks: God invites his people to call to him and promises to show them great things. Ask what you have stopped calling to God about. And ask what sounds of ordinary joy you long to hear again in your home or town.

passages.t: A righteous Branch, and a covenant as sure as day and night
passages.happening:
The days are coming when God will fulfill his good promise to Israel and Judah (verse 14). He will cause a righteous Branch to sprout for David, who will do justice and righteousness in the land (verse 15). Judah will be saved and Jerusalem live securely, and the city will be called ‘The LORD Our Righteousness’ (verse 16).

David will never lack a man on the throne of Israel (verse 17), nor will the Levitical priests lack a man to offer before God (verse 18). If anyone could break God's covenant with day and night so that they no longer came at their time, then his covenant with David and the Levites could be broken (verses 20 and 21). As the stars and the sand cannot be counted, so God will multiply David's descendants and the Levites (verse 22).

People are saying that the LORD has rejected the two families he chose (verse 24). God answers that only if he had not set the order of day and night and heaven and earth would he reject the descendants of Jacob and David. ‘For I will restore them from captivity and will have compassion on them’ (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
Verses 15 and 16 repeat the promise of 23:5-6 with a difference. There the king was given that name. Here the city is. King and city share it.

This passage, verses 14 to 26, is missing from the Greek translation of Jeremiah. It is the longest part of the Hebrew book with no Greek counterpart. Some scholars think it was added to the Hebrew in the exile or after, as a renewed promise to David's line and the priests; others think the Greek translator or his source left it out.

The two families of verse 24 are probably Israel and Judah, or the line of David and the priests. People were saying God had thrown them away. God answers by pointing to the sky. As long as morning and evening come, his promise stands.
passages.later: A psalm swears the same: ‘Once and for all I have sworn by My holiness’ (Psalm 89:35), and God will not lie to David. Jeremiah 23:5-6 first gave the Branch's name.
passages.hard:
God promised that David would never lack a man on the throne and the Levites would never lack a priest to offer sacrifices. How is that kept, when Judah lost its king and the temple's offerings ended?

The difficulty is real, and readers handle it in several ways. Christians have traditionally said the promises are fulfilled in Christ, who is both the eternal king of David's line and the high priest whose once-for-all sacrifice ends the need for animal offerings (Hebrews 7 to 10); some add that believers now share a royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:5, 9). Some Christian interpreters, especially dispensational ones, expect a future literal restoration involving Israel, drawing on Ezekiel 40 to 48. Jewish tradition has generally understood the promises as awaiting the Messiah and the rebuilt temple, with prayer and Torah study standing in for sacrifice in the meantime.

The promise says David will not lack a man, not that a king will sit on the throne without a break; the line went on, with Jehoiachin released (52:31-34) and his grandson Zerubbabel leading the return. All readers agree that God's covenant with his people stands as firmly as day and night.
passages.asks: God points to day and night as the measure of his faithfulness. Ask what promise of God you have doubted because it seemed broken. And ask what it would look like to read each morning as a sign that his word still stands.
